title: How Learning Board was built, step by step
oneLine: Start from a proven canvas, add the hard part (shape recognition) with tests first, then the gestures, the learning tools, saving, and finally polish from real use.

nodes.label: 1. Move it out
nodes.sub: its own folder and git repo

steps.say: The old lesson board moved out of the work project into its own folder, made into a git repo so friends can clone it.
Drawing engines take years. Instead of writing one, it uses Excalidraw, an open-source canvas, and spends the effort on what is new.
The hardest part first: turning a shaky stroke into the shape it meant. Tests came with it — 200 wobbly drawings of each shape must be recognised at least 95% of the time.
Then the gestures that trigger it, the way pro apps do: pause at the end of a stroke, or double-click it later.
A line from one shape to another becomes an arrow attached to both; handwriting can become neat text.
The learning tools: dots flowing along arrows, steps with notes, Play with pulses, ticks, crosses and quiz cards.
Boards are saved in the browser, the app installs and works offline, and a small Node server serves it. Windows and Mac alike.
Every feature was checked with a real mouse in Chrome and screenshots. That caught real bugs: a hidden Play button, arrows bunched in a corner, a last step that never played.
Your feedback shaped the rest: the lessons' hand-drawn look as art styles, the bright green dot, five kinds of flow, a quicker snap with a shake.
And for learning DSA fast: / blocks for arrays, lists, trees, heaps, graphs and hash tables, Tidy to line things up, and hold C to fix your writing.
